Hi Mel — general thoughts only, as I haven’t examined your leg. Morning stiffness, tenderness and a lump a few centimetres above the heel after that jump in volume is a pattern often seen with mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy. That doesn’t confirm the diagnosis or rule out something else online.

I wouldn’t completely rest it by default, but I also wouldn’t just run through it. For now, cut the volume back and drop hills, intervals and anything faster. Flat, easy runs on alternate days are reasonable if they stay within the pain guide below. Limping around the office afterwards suggests yesterday’s dose was too much, so reduce it further.

For strength, heavy, slow calf raises generally have better evidence than heel drops alone. Start at a level you can control, using both straight-knee and bent-knee raises, and gradually add resistance — for example, 3–4 sets of 6–12 reps, three times a week. On more irritable days, use gentler isometric holds instead: push the midfoot into the floor without moving the heel, around 5 holds of 30–45 seconds. Heel drops can still be useful, but I wouldn’t begin by dropping aggressively into a deep stretch off a step.

A useful loading guide is discomfort up to about 3/10, provided it has settled back to its usual level by the next morning and morning stiffness isn’t progressively worsening. More pain, a longer flare or increased limping means reduce the running or exercise load.

I’d avoid stretching it “until it burns”. Cortisone injections around the Achilles are also generally avoided because they can weaken the tendon; it isn’t simply a quick-fix needle. Also mention any recent fluoroquinolone antibiotics, such as ciprofloxacin, to your GP or physio, as these can be associated with tendon problems. Don’t stop prescribed antibiotics without speaking to the prescriber.

If there’s a sudden pop, a sensation of being kicked in the back of the leg, or you suddenly can’t push off properly, stop running **and** the calf exercises and get assessed urgently that day through a GP or ED, as that could indicate a rupture.

Otherwise, if it isn’t clearly settling over the next 3–4 weeks, book with any sports physio near Bayswater for a proper assessment and graded plan — sooner if it’s worsening.
